P1.evidence: Setter notes were read back properly and used — 'I know you spoke with Derek, so I have a bit of a head start on you', then 'if I remember correctly, the goal was about 180, 190?' and 'I saw a current weight. You're 210 right now.' Frame agreement was asked for and given: 'Does that all sound good?' 'Yeah.' The open question was clean: 'walk me through, like, what could we potentially help you with?' The frame itself was three-part — 'where we're at, where we're trying to get to, what's kind of been getting in the way' — with 'what you need' again missing.

P2.evidence: Facts were gathered well and the health question was asked directly, surfacing type 1 diabetes, diastasis recti, medicated hypertension and neuropathy; injuries were probed further than the script requires — 'with the back, do we have any herniated discs or anything?' Hereditary conditions were not asked. The two misses matter more than usual on this prospect: sleep was never asked despite him volunteering a 3am start and up to seven working days a week, and daytime energy was never asked of a 62-year-old type 1 diabetic. Both are frontline diabetes indicators and both were left on the table.

P3.evidence: The bridge was run — 'you talked about losing a of weight, but why are we actually wanting to do that?' — and one good follow-up landed real material: 'What's been happening on the self-image and self-esteem?' producing 'when I look at my profile in a window, it's very upsetting.' It was then dropped. The goal set never moved past weight: mobility, strength and energy were never offered as alternatives, and 'something physical you want to do but can't' was never asked of a man who quit Taekwondo because he feared injuring himself. The impact question was only glancing — 'have you chatted with the missus about this much?' — and there was no reflection back. The rep moved from self-esteem straight to money in under ninety seconds.

P4.evidence: The strongest phase in the call. Every past attempt was surfaced and worked — the gym, Taekwondo, the nutritionist, the physical therapist, teenage walking — with real follow-through: 'why did you discontinue it?', 'what held you back from sticking to Taekwondo since you were getting results from it?', 'what's actually been missing from you getting the results that you've wanted?' The prospect named his own gap twice: 'I think some kind of structured, more structured, consistent exercise' and 'the diet piece is also a factor'. P4f is partial because the rep asserted the root cause rather than asking it — 'as soon as we stop paying the personal trainer, we just fall back into old habits' — instead of making the prospect say it.

P5.evidence: The two-year question was asked properly — 'if you didn't make a change and you didn't get this figured out, like, what would life look like in two, three, four years?' — and the answer was the most consequential material available: 'it's very bad for my, as a diabetic, and it's very bad for my health.' The rep did not press it. He never asked whether that was acceptable to settle for or why not, so the consequence was stated and never made to land. The line-in-the-sand move ran and got a yes: 'it's kind of sounding like it's time to draw a line in the sand and get this thing handled.'

P6.evidence: Not run in any form. Straight after the line-in-the-sand yes the rep introduced the money problem himself — 'And then also cost is going to come into a factor' — and spent the rest of the call qualifying the prospect out. No belief question, no all-in question, and the presentation was never actually delivered, so the sequence the script protects was inverted: affordability was tested before value was established.

P11.evidence: No close was attempted on the six-month programme; the rep pre-empted it and then accepted the decline. A separate transaction was attempted on the lower-priced Primal University product — a link was sent live and the prospect was told 'you can just punch in your card and get rock and roll' — but none of the P11 steps apply to it: there is no Trevor onboarding call, no agreement to sign, and the Skool community is the product itself rather than an onboarding step.

objection_plays.detail: The money trigger was overwhelming and arrived early — 'money is definitely a thing', 'It is paycheck to paycheck', 'right now, no'. One element of the play ran: 'financially, we're literally a couple hundred bucks expendable each month, or what are we actually looking at month to month in terms of discretionary income?' Everything else was skipped. There was no isolation question, no 'you're not in a should-I place, you're in a how place' reframe, no offer to explore making it work, and none of the rest of the financial picture — cash on hand, number of cards, available credit per card, used versus available, crypto or investments. More significantly the rep ran the play backwards: rather than isolating and then opening the wallet, he told the prospect the programme was probably out of reach before the prospect had refused.

'whatever it is, I'd have to, you know, even if it's less, I'd still have to think about it' is a think-about-it trigger in substance. No move from the play was attempted — not 'do you feel what we've gone through can get you there', not 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is'. It passed without acknowledgement.

SCRIPT GAP — CLINICAL FIT. The prospect disclosed type 1 diabetes, diastasis recti under active physical therapy, medicated hypertension, diabetic neuropathy and undiagnosed loading-dependent back pain, and there is no scripted path for any of it. The only screening move available to the rep was to ask the prospect for his own opinion, which he did — 'Does any of that prevent working out or limit working out at all?' — and the answer 'No, not from my experience' closed the topic. Nothing in the playbook tells a rep to seek clinician clearance, to treat an abdominal wall separation as a contraindication for loaded and ballistic work, or to decline. This is the same gap the ICP observations already record, and it is the most consequential one in the corpus.

SCRIPT GAP — INCOME QUALIFICATION ASKED OF US. The prospect raised a competitor advertising a $150,000 income floor and asked, in effect, whether Primal has the same criterion: 'for all I know, you may have the same exact criteria. I don't know.' There is no scripted answer for a prospect who asks whether he qualifies, and the rep gave none — the question was simply never returned to.

SCRIPT GAP — A CHEAPER SUBSTITUTE THAT WORKED. The prospect has twice lost weight on essentially free methods: a 25-minute daily fast walk as a teenager and Taekwondo two summers ago. He also had a $60/month gym he cancelled and a $10/month gym across the street he considered. Objection C assumes capacity to pay is the blocker; here the blocker is a functioning low-cost substitute. The rep argued the point well and off-script — the identity-change and external-accountability argument — but had no play to run and ultimately conceded the price.
No spouse objection. His wife is working on the same goals alongside him and was framed as an ally.
No timing objection was raised; the blocker stated was money throughout.
No fear or doubt about the programme, though he did mention having quit Taekwondo partly through fear of injuring himself — never explored.

notes: Discovery and root cause were genuinely good and the rep built a real picture. The call was then lost in Phase 6, which never happened: the rep introduced affordability himself, before establishing value and before any commitment check, and from that point was arguing his way out of the deal rather than into it. Coach the sequence — value, commitment, then price — and coach not raising the objection on the prospect's behalf. Separately and more importantly, this call needed a clinical stop that the script does not contain and the rep did not improvise.
